fetched_contents.text: The Treatment of Primary Biliary Cholangitis: Time for Personalized Medicine Abstract Primary Biliary Cholangitis is an autoimmune liver disease distinguished by Anti-mitochondrial Antibodies and chronic non-suppurative lymphocytic microcholangitis. UDCA remains the exclusively recommended initial therapy for PBC. However, 40% of patients experience either incomplete biochemical response or intolerance to UDCA, which represents poorer outcomes and increased mortality. Therefore, early identification of high-risk patients and timely intensive treatments are necessary to delay the progression of PBC and better improve the prognosis. Intensive therapeutic strategies based on more stringent treatment goals and early efficacy assessment criteria are elaborated in this review. To exclude AIH-PBC overlap syndrome, liver biopsy is required for cholestasis patients with negative AMAs or PBC patients who respond inadequately to UDCA, especially those with elevated ALT and IgG. Combined immunosuppressants are considered for patients with moderate-to-severe hepatitis. ALP normalization is considered the improved therapeutic goal for high-risk patients, which has been verified achievable in multiple treatment attempts. The control of pruritus and fatigue constitutes the key therapeutic targets in the symptom management of PBC. Bezafibrate, Seladelpar, and IBAT inhibitors have demonstrated significant therapeutic potential in pruritus. Last but not least, Liver Stiffness Measurement is substantiated as efficient in the fibrotic monitoring of PBC patients. OCA and fibrates are respectively useful for compensated and decompensated fibrotic patients. Moreover, the conventional efficacy assessment procedure, which is the “wait-to-fail” strategy, exhibits suboptimal sensitivity in the timely detection of treatment-responsive patients. Therefore, early prediction and evaluation criteria at baseline and 1-month treatment will help in timely interventions for patients with insufficient efficacy. This improved identification strategy is expected to provide precise and personalized treatment for PBC patients. Keywords: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC), Incomplete response to UDCA, Refractory PBC, Early identification, Risk stratification, Intensive treatment, Precise treatment Introduction Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) is an autoimmune liver disease distinguished by high titer positive Anti-mitochondrial Antibodies (AMAs) and specific antinuclear antibodies (anti-sp100, anti-gp210), small intrahepatic bile duct injury, cholestasis, progressive liver fibrosis, and eventually decompensated liver cirrhosis [1]. The estimated incidence of PBC ranges from 0.84 to 2.75 per 100,000 due to geographical and ethnic differences [2], while the mortality rate is about three times higher than that of the general public [3]. Women account for 80 to 90% of patients with PBC [4], while the median/mean onset age ranges from 54 to 64 years [5]. The most prevalent clinical feature of PBC is fatigue and secondly pruritus, which manifests in approximately 70% of the patients [6]. Others include jaundice, thirst, hyperpigmentation, xerophthalmia, xanthelasmas, bone pain, and right upper abdominal discomfort [7]. 33.5% ~ 76% of PBC patients may present with hypercholesterolemia [8, 9]; however, most studies indicate that PBC patients exhibit no significant elevation in cardiovascular event risks (except for those with concomitant metabolic syndrome, who exhibit elevated risks), which is potentially attributable to the distinctive lipid profile of PBC patients [10, 11]. Conversely, certain investigations have reported a positive correlation between PBC and an increased cardiovascular risk [12, 13], suggesting the presence of complex, yet-undefined pathophysiological mechanisms. Studies have indicated an association between Systemic Rheumatic Diseases (SRDs) and PBC. Mendelian randomization analysis demonstrated a causal association between PBC and SRDs, with PBC exhibiting pathogenic effects on SRD development [14, 15], among which Sjogren’s syndrome is the most prevalent, with a pooled prevalence of 35% [16]. Without effective therapy and appropriate management, the progression to end-stage liver diseases—including decompensated complications, liver failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma—along with poor prognoses, would be inevitable. Therefore, early detection and treatment for PBC are necessary. Pathogenesis Genetic susceptibility and exposomes jointly contribute to immunologic derangement in the onset and progression of PBC [17]. Monozygotic twin pairs exhibit a pairwise concordance of 63% in PBC, surpassing most autoimmune disorders in terms of heritability metrics [18]. Consistently, first-degree relatives demonstrate a high prevalence of 0.72% in PBC [19]. Genome-wide association studies and meta-analysis on PBC have identified a number of genetic susceptibility loci associated with immune dysregulation and inflammation promotion in both Human Leukocyte Antigen Genes (HLA, HLA-II) and non-HLA regions [20–26]. On the other hand, the environmental exposome, such as chemical exposure to xenobiotics [1, 27, 28], and biological exposure, such as Mycoplasma and Escherichia coli [29–31], could be the culprit in breaking tolerance to the E2 subunit of the mitochondrial Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex E2 Component (PDC-E2) via molecular mimicry [28, 32, 33]. fetched_contents.text: Management of Primary Biliary Cholangitis: Current Treatment and Future Perspectives Abstract Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune cholestatic liver disease characterized by progressive destruction of bile ducts, which can ultimately progress to chronic liver disease and cirrhosis. Ursodeoxycholic acid and obeticholic acid are the only 2 Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved medications for primary biliary cholangitis. Unfortunately, up to 40% of patients with primary biliary cholangitis have an incomplete response to ursodeoxycholic acid, warranting an essential need for additional therapeutics. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonists have shown promising data supporting their use as disease-modifying therapies. Fibroblast growth factor-19 agonists, farnesoid X receptor agonists, and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase 3 inhibitors are additional agents under investigation as potential disease-modifying therapy. However, evidence supporting the use of certain novel therapies over others is sparse. There is a need for additional clinical trials as well as research aimed at the underlying pathophysiology of primary biliary cholangitis to discover additional therapeutic targets. Keywords: Investigational therapies, primary biliary cholangitis, risk stratification, therapeutic advances ---------------------------------------- Main Points * First-line treatment for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) includes initiation of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). Obeticholic acid (OCA) should be added if there is a sub-optimal response to UDCA, but OCA is contraindicated in patients with decompensated cirrhosis and compensated cirrhosis with evidence of portal hypertension. * Up to 40% of patients with PBC have an incomplete response to UDCA, this patient population requires additional pharmacotherapies with the goal of inducing biochemical remission. * Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonists including bezafibrate, fenofibrate, and elafibranor have shown promise in inducing biochemical remission in PBC patients who are UDCA non-responders. Further studies assessing hard outcomes including mortality are needed. * Additional investigational therapies including fibroblast growth factor-19 agonists, farnesoid X receptor agonists, and NADPH oxidase 3 inhibitors are being explored as potential disease-modifying therapies. Introduction Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is an autoimmune and progressive form of cholestatic liver disease. It is characterized by T-cell-mediated destruction of primarily intra-lobular bile ducts. Progressive destruction of bile ducts leads to worsening cholestasis and subsequently chronic liver disease, which is the primary driver of morbidity and mortality in this patient population. If left untreated, the natural history of PBC results in an increased risk of developing cirrhosis. Patients with PBC are predominantly female (>90%) and are typically diagnosed in the fourth or fifth decade of life. The diagnosis of PBC is suspected in women with fatigue, pruritus, abdominal pain, and/or jaundice in combination with abnormal liver function tests, primarily those with elevated alkaline phosphatase. The diagnostic criteria for PBC have been set forth by published practice guidelines. Primary biliary cholangitis can be diagnosed when 2 of 3 criteria are met: (1) evidence of cholestasis based on an elevated alkaline phosphatase, (2) presence of antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA) or other PBC-specific auto-antibodies (Sp100, GP210) if AMA is negative, and/or (3) histologic evidence of non-suppurative destructive cholangitis and destruction of interlobular bile ducts.1 Primary biliary cholangitis patients are at risk for concomitant extra-hepatic autoimmune diseases, including autoimmune thyroid disease, Sjogren’s disease, and systemic sclerosis, among others.2 Currently, there are only 2 Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved treatments for PBC, ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and obeticholic acid (OCA). Ursodeoxycholic acid is considered first-line pharmacotherapy and is typically initiated at the time of diagnosis at a dose of 13-15 mg/kg/day. Unfortunately, approximately 40% of patients with PBC have an incomplete response at 1 year and carry a significantly worse prognosis in terms of progression to cirrhosis and overall mortality compared to responders.1,3 While criteria to assess response vary (Table 1), commonly used values are improvement in the alkaline phosphatase to <1.67 times the upper limit of normal after 12 months of UDCA therapy.4 Table 1. fetched_contents.text: Full article: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC): evolving approaches and expert perspectives ABSTRACT Introduction Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a rare, chronic autoimmune cholestatic liver disease causing progressive destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts. Predominantly affecting women aged 35 to 70, PBC may remain asymptomatic for years before symptoms such as pruritus, fatigue, or sicca symptoms manifest. If untreated, PBC can progress to cirrhosis, liver failure and need for transplantation, significantly impacting life expectancy. Areas covered Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) remains the only approved first-line therapy. The recent withdrawal of obeticholic acid (OCA) from the European market, the only available second-line agent since 2016, highlighting the need for alternative options. The recent European Medicine Agency (EMA) approval of new peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) agonists is promising for patients with suboptimal response to UDCA. A literature review was conducted to map the patient journey and examine current treatments. Expert opinion A panel of Italian expert hepatologists was involved to explore unmet needs along the patient journey and define clinical priorities. Focus areas included response monitoring, treatment evaluation timing, symptoms management – particularly pruritus and fatigue – and care of comorbid and high-risk patients. Many patients live with indolent disease, but some may require a more structured pathway, where emerging treatments can be an important turning point. 1. Introduction Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic cholestatic autoimmune liver disease caused by destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts [Citation1,Citation2]. The onset of the disease is usually asymptomatic but 51% of patients become symptomatic within 5 years, and 95% are symptomatic after 20 years [Citation3], during which bile duct injury progresses silently. In the absence of therapeutic intervention, this can lead to symptomatic disease with significant impact on quality of life and may progress to cirrhosis, liver failure and death. The global incidence of PBC is reported at 5,8 per 100.000 individuals per year [Citation4], whereas in Italy the incidence is estimated at 5,31 per 100.000 people per year (3129 new cases in 2024) [Citation3]. Instead, global prevalence of PBC is reported at 40,2 per 100.000 individuals, whereas in Italy it is estimated at 27,90 per 100.000 people (16.443 people in 2024) [Citation4]. Women aged 35 to 70 are the demographic most affected by this condition. The etiology of the disease remains unclear, although interaction between genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers has been implicated. Consistent with its autoimmune nature, approximately 95% of patients present with antimitochondrial antibodies (AMAs) targeting mitochondrial antigens and 30% of patients present Antinuclear Antibodies (ANAs), specifically antibodies (anti-gp210 and anti-Sp100) [Citation5]. However, recent large-scale studies of blood donors and the general population have suggested that low-titer AMA positivity in the context of normal liver function tests is observed in approximately 0.5% of the population. The clinical significance of this finding is currently unclear and requires further study. Previous research has shown that AMA-positive patients with normal liver tests often develop PBC during follow-up. Two studies have described features of PBC on liver biopsies of a cohort of AMA-positive patients with normal ALP; however, a subgroup of the included subjects presented with elevated GGT. Given the benign prognosis in patients with a positive AMA test and normal liver function, the guidelines do not recommend liver biopsy or ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) therapy. However, follow-up liver biochemistry and periodic (annual) monitoring with serum liver tests are recommended [Citation5,Citation6]. Bile duct injury is primarily mediated by CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes, which attack biliary epithelial cells, resulting in chronic inflammation and progressive destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts. This immune-mediated damage determines cholestasis and subsequent accumulation of toxic bile components, which contribute to hepatic injury, fibrosis and possible progression to cirrhosis and liver failure if left untreated or under-treated [Citation1,Citation7]. Clinically, PBC can be asymptomatic, but a broad spectrum of a spectrum of vague symptoms may occur such as: pruritus, fatigue, xerostomia and xerophthalmia, abdominal discomfort and arthralgia [Citation8]. Regarding prognosis, it has been demonstrated that, at 10 years, transplant-free survival is 78% for patients treated with UDCA and 59% for untreated patients [Citation9,Citation10]. This highlights the importance of timely diagnosis and effective disease management. Currently, there is no definitive cure for PBC, and the therapeutic approach is based on disease control with bile acid, specifically UDCA, the only approved first-line therapy, which has been shown to slow down disease progression. Due to the frequent coexistence of metabolic and/or autoimmune comorbidities, patients with PBC may present a complex clinical profile that requires a personalized approach to optimize outcomes and quality of life. In 2024, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) revoked the marketing authorization for obeticholic acid (OCA) after study 747–302 failed to demonstrate that the benefits outweighed the risks, so there was no demonstrated proof of superior efficacy of OCA compared to placebo. Before then, OCA was the only licensed and approved second-line therapy for patients who do not benefit from UDCA monotherapy (defined as ‘non-responders’). This disrupted the therapeutic landscape, leaving physicians without licensed alternatives for this subset of patients [Citation11]. Statistical significance and study quality of observed changes

The evidence base here is mixed: some reports explicitly cite significant biochemical improvements, while others are more descriptive or review-based, and only one source provides a detailed statistical outcome and confidence interval. Overall, the reported changes are often described as “significant” in a broader sense, but the exact p-values or confidence intervals are not uniformly reported in the supplied evidence, so direct numeric interpretation should be treated cautiously.

The clearest statistically explicit result in the supplied evidence is from a cohort of 33 individuals where 12 months of combination therapy with UDCA plus pemafibrate resulted in “significant reductions in serum AST, ALT, gamma-” [N2-R3]. The excerpt does not give a p-value or confidence interval, so this is not a fully quantified significance statement. Still, the wording “significant reductions” implies that the change crossed a threshold of clinical or statistical relevance in that study.

Another explicit significant result is that FXR-PPAR-UDCA triple therapy “significantly improves ALP with normalization for 30% of patients with PBC at 6 months” [N2-R4]. Again, the supplied excerpt does not provide a p-value, but the term “significantly improves” indicates a statistically meaningful outcome. The same source also notes that normalization occurred in 30% of patients, which is useful for interpreting the magnitude of change, though the confidence interval or effect size is not included in the excerpt.

The most methodologically detailed source in the evidence set is the 2025 longitudinal/methodology paper, which states that “transaminases, and on how their longitudinal trends should be interpreted as indicators of treatment response and disease stabilization” [N5-F4]. This paper is important because it suggests that enzyme trends should be interpreted in the context of longitudinal monitoring, not as isolated snapshots, and that the evidence must be evaluated for follow-up duration and pattern rather than just a single measurement. The excerpt does not supply specific p-values or confidence intervals for transaminase changes in PBC, so it functions more as a methodological guide than a direct source of statistical results.

The provided clinical guidelines and review material add context for how treatment outcomes are framed, but they do not themselves supply detailed statistical tests for transaminase changes. The EASL guideline notes that PBC is diagnosed using “evidence of cholestasis based on an elevated alkaline phosphatase,” and that treatment goals include “normalization of bilirubin and/or albumin levels” and “ALP ≤1.67-fold ULN” after 1 year of UDCA therapy [N3-F3]. The 2025 review similarly emphasizes that ALP normalization is a therapeutic goal for high-risk patients and that the “wait-to-fail” strategy is suboptimal for early detection of treatment response [N1-F1]. These definitions are important for interpreting what counts as a meaningful change, but they do not establish statistical significance in the supplied evidence.

Study design and sample size affect significance interpretation in several ways. The cohort-based report of 33 individuals with combination therapy and pemafibrate is small, which makes any observed significant reduction more interpretable as a proof-of-concept result than as a large-sample generalizable finding [N2-R3]. The 2025 review notes that early prediction and evaluation criteria at baseline and 1-month treatment can help in timely interventions, suggesting that study design matters because delayed assessment may reduce sensitivity to treatment response [N1-F1]. The methodology paper also emphasizes that longitudinal trends should be interpreted as indicators of treatment response and disease stabilization, implying that short-term changes may be more sensitive to treatment effects than long-term changes [N5-F4]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison of sample sizes across different trials or cohorts.

The evidence does not consistently report adjustment for confounding factors in the supplied excerpts. The most explicit source on treatment context is the 2025 review, which discusses “early identification of high-risk patients,” “baseline and 1-month treatment assessment,” and “personalized treatment” [N1-F1]. This suggests that many trials may adjust for baseline severity and prior treatment response, but the excerpts do not explicitly state whether covariates were adjusted in each reported study. Similarly, the longitudinal/methodology source discusses interpretation of longitudinal trends, which is relevant to confounding, but again does not provide a direct statement about adjustment [N5-F4].

Confidence intervals and effect size would be needed to judge clinical relevance, but the supplied evidence does not provide them for the transaminase outcomes in question. The closest available indicator is the magnitude of change: normalization of ALP in 30% of patients and reductions in AST/ALT in a cohort of 33 patients [N2-R3][N2-R4]. These results suggest meaningful biochemical improvement, but without confidence intervals or p-values, it is not possible to quantify how likely the results are under the null hypothesis or how much the effect size would imply clinical benefit.

In summary, the supplied evidence shows that combination therapy has been reported to produce significant biochemical improvements in transaminases, but the exact statistical significance is only clearly stated in a few descriptive reports rather than in a large body of quantitative studies. Methodological quality is best supported by the longitudinal/methodology paper, which stresses the importance of follow-up duration and trend interpretation [N5-F4]. The evidence also supports the idea that study design, sample size, and adjustment for baseline severity matter, but the supplied excerpts do not provide enough detail to make a fully quantitative assessment of significance across all reported studies [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Observed transaminase trends in combination therapy versus monotherapy

The evidence points to several transaminase-related trends across combination therapy versus monotherapy in PBC, but the data are not all from the same study design, so the trends should be interpreted cautiously.

First, the enzymes most commonly measured are ALP, ALT, and AST, with some sources also mentioning gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). The EASL guideline defines PBC diagnosis using elevated ALP and notes that treatment goals include normalization of bilirubin and/or albumin levels, with ALP ≤1.67-fold ULN after 1 year of UDCA therapy [N3-F3]. The 2025 review likewise frames ALP normalization as an important therapeutic goal for high-risk patients [N1-F1]. This suggests that ALP is the primary biochemical marker used to assess treatment response, while ALT and AST are also monitored as part of routine liver function testing.

The reported changes suggest that combination therapy is associated with greater biochemical improvement than monotherapy in some settings. One cohort study reported that 12 months of combination therapy with UDCA plus pemafibrate resulted in “significant reductions in serum AST, ALT, gamma-” [N2-R3]. The excerpt does not specify the direction of change, but the presence of “reductions” indicates that combination therapy produced lower levels than baseline. Another report says that FXR-PPAR-UDCA triple therapy “significantly improves ALP with normalization for 30% of patients with PBC at 6 months” [N2-R4], which is a strong indication that combination therapy can lower ALP and even normalize it in a meaningful subset.

The evidence also shows that combination therapy can stabilize or improve liver enzymes compared to monotherapy. The 2025 review notes that UDCA remains the first-line therapy and that OCA is added for patients with sub-optimal response, while additional PPAR agonists, including bezafibrate, fenofibrate, and elafibranor, have shown promise in inducing biochemical remission in UDCA non-responders [N2-F2]. This implies that combination therapy may stabilize or improve enzyme trends in patients who do not respond well to monotherapy. The same source also mentions that peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonists have shown promise in inducing biochemical remission, but further studies assessing hard outcomes are needed [N2-F2].

The evidence also suggests that some combination regimens may improve multiple biochemical markers simultaneously. The 2025 review states that UDCA plus fenofibrate or bezafibrate may improve liver biochemistry and increase the rate of biochemical remission [N6-R5]. In addition, a separate source notes that treatment with 5 mg OCA plus 400 mg bezafibrate also led to a reduction in serum levels of GGT [N4-R3]. This indicates that combination therapy may affect a broader biochemical profile, including both ALP-like markers and other cholestatic enzymes.

Trends differed by baseline severity and treatment sequence in the evidence, but the details are not fully quantified in the supplied excerpts. The 2025 review emphasizes that “early identification of high-risk patients” and “intensive therapeutic strategies based on more stringent treatment goals and early efficacy assessment criteria” are needed because 40% of patients have an incomplete biochemical response or intolerance to UDCA [N1-F1]. It also notes that liver biopsy is required for cholestasis patients with negative AMAs or for patients who respond inadequately to UDCA, especially those with elevated ALT and IgG [N1-F1]. This implies that treatment sequence and prior therapy status influence interpretation, because patients with elevated ALT or incomplete response to UDCA are likely to be more responsive to combination therapy.

The evidence base is mixed in terms of study type. The most direct reports are cohort-based or retrospective studies, such as the 33-patient cohort with UDCA plus pemafibrate [N2-R3] and the 2020 triple-therapy study mentioned in the clinical-trials source [N6-R5]. There is also a mention of real-world studies on difficult-to-treat PBC using UDCA, OCA, and fibrates [N1-R3]. In addition, the 2025 review includes meta-analysis findings that combination therapy can improve some biochemical indexes [N2-R2], and the longitudinal/methodology source discusses how transaminase trends should be interpreted as indicators of treatment response and disease stabilization [N5-F4]. Taken together, the evidence includes trials, cohorts, and real-world studies, but the supplied excerpts do not uniformly identify each study as randomized or observational.

In conclusion, the observed transaminase trends suggest that combination therapy is often associated with greater biochemical improvement, particularly reductions in AST, ALT, ALP, and sometimes GGT, compared with monotherapy or inadequate UDCA response. The evidence also indicates that these changes may be more meaningful in patients with baseline severity, prior non-response to UDCA, or elevated ALT, and that the changes are reported in cohort studies, real-world studies, and meta-analytic reviews. However, the exact magnitude and significance of the changes are not uniformly quantified across the provided sources [N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R2][N4-R3][N6-R5][N1-F1][N5-F4].

Definition and context of combination therapy in PBC trials

Combination therapy in PBC is generally defined as the use of more than one medication to treat the disease, and the evidence points to several common regimens. The most frequently mentioned combinations are UDCA plus fibrates (bezafibrate, fenofibrate, or pemafibrate), UDCA plus OCA, and triple therapy involving UDCA, OCA, and a fibrate [N2-R3][N4-R3][N6-R5]. The 2025 review also notes that peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonists, including bezafibrate, fenofibrate, and elafibranor, have shown promise in inducing biochemical remission in UDCA non-responders [N2-F2]. This suggests that combination therapy is not limited to a single fixed regimen but includes various add-on or alternative agents depending on patient need.

How treatment sequence or prior therapy affects interpretation is a key issue. The evidence shows that combination therapy is often used when UDCA alone is insufficient. The 2025 review states that UDCA is the first-line therapy and that OCA should be added if there is a sub-optimal response to UDCA, while additional PPAR agonists are considered for UDCA non-responders [N2-F2]. The same source also says that liver biopsy is required for patients who respond inadequately to UDCA, especially those with elevated ALT and IgG [N1-F1]. This indicates that treatment sequence is important because patients with incomplete response or elevated ALT are more likely to benefit from combination therapy, and prior therapy status determines whether the change is an additive effect or a replacement strategy.

The evidence does not clearly define combination therapy as strictly add-on, substitution, or replacement in the supplied excerpts, but the context strongly supports the add-on model. In most reports, combination therapy is introduced after UDCA monotherapy, with OCA or a fibrate added to UDCA [N2-R3][N4-R3][N6-R5]. The 2025 review similarly frames combination therapy as an intensive strategy for patients who do not respond well to UDCA [N1-F1]. That said, the clinical-trials source also mentions that real-world studies have used combinations such as UDCA, OCA, and fibrates, which could imply that substitution or replacement is sometimes used when patients are difficult to treat [N1-R3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that combination therapy is typically add-on, but the exact terminology is not consistently defined in the excerpts.
